identity.answer: This sheep has black wool.

spawning.answer: You can dye a sheep black. Natural wool colors use their own spawning distribution; not every dyed color has a natural biome-exclusive flock.

shearing.answer: Shearing gives black wool while leaving the adult sheep alive. Eating grass can regrow its wool.

identity.answer: A rainbow sheep uses the special jeb_ name appearance.

naming.answer: Name a sheep jeb_ using a name tag. Its displayed wool cycles through colors.

drops.answer: The rainbow appearance does not change the sheep’s underlying wool color or the wool color you harvest.

shearing.answer: Shearing a jeb_ sheep gives its underlying wool color, not a changing rainbow item.

spawning.answer: Find shulkers on End-city walls and End ships on the outer End islands. They generate with those structures.

drops.answer: In Bedrock, shulkers can drop shulker shells with a quantity-based Looting increase.

breeding.answer: Shulkers do not breed with food. They can duplicate through suitable shulker-bullet interactions, including a special Bedrock behavior when a shulker bullet kills one.

combat.answer: Their homing bullets inflict Levitation, making the eventual fall dangerous. A closed shell provides protection, and shulkers can teleport away when hurt.

interactions.answer: Shulkers can be dyed in Bedrock. Their shell color is separate from the shell item they drop.

taming.answer: Shulker cannot be tamed as player-owned pets. You can still ask how to breed them.

teleportation.answer: A shulker can teleport when its attachment or position becomes unsuitable and under some combat conditions. A name tag does not disable that movement. Keep suitable nearby attachment surfaces in mind rather than assuming one small enclosure guarantees it stays put.

variants.answer: Shulkers can have different shell colors, and open or close their shells. In Bedrock, using dye on a shulker to change its color requires Creative mode.

equipment.answer: In Bedrock, you can change a shulker’s shell color by using dye on it in Creative mode. It is not a Survival dye interaction.

spawn_conditions.answer: End-city generation supplies the original shulkers; an empty city does not normally refill by waiting. Additional shulkers can come from special shulker-bullet duplication mechanics, not ordinary animal breeding or a dark End platform.

experience.answer: It gives 5 experience points after a player or tamed-wolf kill. Looting affects certain item drops, not this experience reward.

attack_style.answer: A shulker opens its shell and fires a guided bullet that causes Levitation. It can teleport when threatened.

provocation.answer: Shulkers are hostile to players they detect. Their closed shell protects them more than their open state.

counterplay.answer: Destroy incoming bullets or use cover. In Bedrock a shield can stop the bullet’s damage while Levitation still applies, so prepare a safe landing rather than assuming the shield prevents the effect.

lifetime.answer: Shulkers do not naturally despawn, including in Peaceful. They can teleport, so a missing shulker may have moved rather than despawned. Persistence does not mean it cannot be killed.

growth.answer: A shulker has no normal baby form that grows into an adult. There is no ordinary baby-growth timer or growth food to use for this mob.

relocation.answer: A minecart can carry a shulker in Bedrock. Bring an empty cart into contact with it, then use rails and powered rails along a protected route. An active activator rail can eject the passenger. It can still be dangerous while riding; a cart is not taming or protection from its attacks. The cart alone does not guarantee persistence in Bedrock.

identity.answer: A shulker is a hostile shell-covered mob found in End cities. Its projectiles cause Levitation, and its shells are used to craft portable shulker boxes.

behavior.answer: A shulker is a hostile shell-covered mob found in End cities. Its projectiles cause Levitation, and its shells are used to craft portable shulker boxes.

health.answer: Its normal maximum health is 30 health points (15 hearts). Effects can change its health during play.

fire.answer: It is immune to ordinary fire and lava damage. That does not protect it from every other kind of damage.

sunlight.answer: Ordinary sunlight does not make it take burning damage. It is fire-immune, although other environmental hazards can still matter.

spawning.answer: Shulkers fire homing bullets at targets.

combat.answer: A shulker bullet can cause Levitation. Destroy or avoid it and prepare for the fall if hit. These are not collectible ammunition items.

projectile_use.answer: A shulker fires guided bullets that track their target. These are not ordinary arrows.

projectile_effects.answer: A hit applies Levitation. In Bedrock a shield can block damage while Levitation still applies.

retrieval.answer: A bullet can be destroyed by hitting it or by collision with blocks. It does not turn into a collectible ammunition item.

identity.answer: A shulker bullet is a homing projectile fired by a shulker. A hit can cause Levitation; destroy it or use cover to avoid being lifted into a dangerous fall.

behavior.answer: A shulker bullet is a homing projectile fired by a shulker. A hit can cause Levitation; destroy it or use cover to avoid being lifted into a dangerous fall.

spawning.answer: Find silverfish in infested blocks, stronghold End-portal-room spawners and certain trial spawners. The Infested effect can also produce them.

drops.answer: Silverfish have no normal item drops; a player or tamed-wolf kill gives experience.

combat.answer: Damaging one can wake nearby silverfish hidden in infested blocks. Avoid carelessly mining through an infested cluster during a fight.

interactions.answer: Breaking an infested block normally releases a silverfish, but Silk Touch can prevent that release. Silverfish and endermites are different mobs.

taming.answer: Silverfish cannot be tamed as player-owned pets.

breeding.answer: You cannot breed a silverfish.

sunlight.answer: Sunlight alone does not make it burn like an exposed zombie or skeleton. Other hazards, such as being out of water or changing dimensions, can still matter for the species.

fire.answer: Without protection, ordinary fire and lava can damage it. Being undead, large, or adapted to a particular biome does not by itself grant fire immunity.

variants.answer: Silverfish can hide in infested blocks and emerge from them. The block is a hiding place, not a baby growth stage.

spawn_conditions.answer: Breaking an infested block without Silk Touch can release silverfish. Stronghold silverfish spawners need light level 11 or less. Trial spawners must be configured for silverfish; ordinary darkness alone is not their natural source.

experience.answer: It gives 5 experience points after a player or tamed-wolf kill. Looting affects certain item drops, not this experience reward.

attack_style.answer: Silverfish bite at close range. If one survives player damage or Poison damage, nearby silverfish can emerge from infested blocks.

provocation.answer: Silverfish are hostile. Mining infested blocks can release them, and attacking a surviving silverfish can turn a small encounter into a group fight.

counterplay.answer: A one-hit kill prevents that silverfish from calling others out of infested blocks. Silk Touch lets you mine infested blocks without releasing their silverfish; avoid slowly poisoning a silverfish beside infested stone.

growth.answer: A silverfish has no normal baby form that grows into an adult. There is no ordinary baby-growth timer or growth food to use for this mob.

lifetime.answer: A naturally spawned silverfish can disappear through ordinary distance despawning unless it has become persistent. In Bedrock, a name tag is one way to prevent ordinary distance despawning; distance rules depend on simulation settings and mob state. A boat or minecart alone is not a blanket persistence guarantee, and persistence does not prevent death.

relocation.answer: A minecart can carry a silverfish in Bedrock. Bring an empty cart into contact with it, then use rails and powered rails along a protected route. An active activator rail can eject the passenger. It can still be dangerous while riding; a cart is not taming or protection from its attacks. The cart alone does not guarantee persistence in Bedrock.

identity.answer: A silverfish is a small hostile mob associated with infested stone and strongholds. Disturbing infested blocks can release it, and nearby infested blocks can make a fight worse.

behavior.answer: A silverfish is a small hostile mob associated with infested stone and strongholds. Disturbing infested blocks can release it, and nearby infested blocks can make a fight worse.

health.answer: Its normal maximum health is 8 health points (4 hearts). Effects can change its health during play.

spawning.answer: Skeletons appear in suitable dark Overworld locations and from certain monster or trial spawners. Nether sources include soul sand valleys and Nether fortresses.

drops.answer: Skeletons can drop bones and arrows, with separate chances for naturally equipped gear. Picked-up equipment has different rules. A charged-creeper kill can produce a skeleton skull.

combat.answer: Skeletons fire arrows and generally burn in daylight unless protected. Use a shield or solid cover and close the distance carefully.

interactions.answer: Keeping an ordinary skeleton in powder snow can convert it into a stray. That does not mean every skeleton-like mob converts the same way.

taming.answer: Skeleton cannot be tamed as player-owned pets.

breeding.answer: You cannot breed a skeleton.

conversion.answer: A normal skeleton kept in powder snow can turn into a stray. This is different from spawning a wither skeleton or bogged.

powder_snow.answer: Keeping a normal skeleton in powder snow can convert it into a stray. Do not assume every skeleton-type mob follows that same conversion rule.

fire.answer: Without protection, ordinary fire and lava can damage it. Being undead, large, or adapted to a particular biome does not by itself grant fire immunity.

variants.answer: Skeletons, strays, wither skeletons, bogged and parched are distinct skeleton-type mobs. They are not all ages or coat colors of an ordinary skeleton.

spawn_conditions.answer: Ordinary skeletons need an eligible dark spawning surface and enough space. Monster rooms and trial spawners are separate sources. Desert and snowy-biome replacement mobs are not simply skeleton coats, and Nether fortress or soul-sand-valley spawning has different context.

experience.answer: The base reward is 5 experience points after a player or tamed-wolf kill. Naturally spawned equipment can affect the total; picked-up equipment and whether the gear itself drops are separate conditions. Looting does not multiply experience.

equipment_drops.answer: Naturally spawned weapons or armor are not guaranteed drops. Qualifying player or tamed-wolf kills and Looting can matter. Equipment the mob picked up later is a different category; do not assume one chance covers both. Its ordinary body loot is separate.

attack_style.answer: A skeleton uses its bow to shoot arrows at its target. Picking up a shield does not mean it can use that shield to block.

provocation.answer: It is a hostile mob that can target players without being hit first. Sunlight can burn an unprotected skeleton, but shade, water or headgear can change that.

counterplay.answer: Use solid cover to interrupt its shots and face incoming arrows with a raised shield. Watch for other attackers while concentrating on the archer.

growth.answer: A skeleton has no normal baby form that grows into an adult. There is no ordinary baby-growth timer or growth food to use for this mob.

lifetime.answer: A naturally spawned skeleton can disappear through ordinary distance despawning unless it has become persistent. In Bedrock, a name tag is one way to prevent ordinary distance despawning; distance rules depend on simulation settings and mob state. A boat or minecart alone is not a blanket persistence guarantee, and persistence does not prevent death.

relocation.answer: A minecart can carry a skeleton in Bedrock. Bring an empty cart into contact with it, then use rails and powered rails along a protected route. An active activator rail can eject the passenger. It can still be dangerous while riding; a cart is not taming or protection from its attacks. The cart alone does not guarantee persistence in Bedrock.

identity.answer: A skeleton is a hostile undead mob that usually fires arrows. Use cover or a shield against it. Ordinary exposed skeletons burn in sunlight unless protected.

behavior.answer: A skeleton is a hostile undead mob that usually fires arrows. Use cover or a shield against it. Ordinary exposed skeletons burn in sunlight unless protected.

health.answer: Its normal maximum health is 20 health points (10 hearts). Effects can change its health during play.

sunlight.answer: It can burn in direct sunlight when unprotected. Shade, water and applicable armor protection can prevent that; sunlight protection does not make it immune to lava.

water.answer: It can breathe underwater.

spawning.answer: Skeleton horses can appear as skeleton traps associated with natural thunderstorms. Approaching a trap can produce several mounted skeleton horsemen; Channeling lightning does not create that natural trap.

drops.answer: A skeleton horse can drop bones under the applicable death conditions. In Bedrock, an untriggered trap horse has no item or experience drops. The skeleton rider has its own separate loot.

taming.answer: In Bedrock, skeleton horses are already tamed. You do not tame them by repeatedly feeding or riding them like an ordinary horse.

breeding.answer: Skeleton horses cannot be bred.

transport.answer: In Bedrock, skeleton horses can be ridden and controlled without a saddle.

combat.answer: The skeleton horse itself is passive. A skeleton horseman is dangerous because of its separate skeleton rider; killing the rider can leave the horse alive.

sunlight.answer: Skeleton horses do not burn in sunlight. Their skeleton riders have separate daylight and protection rules.

equipment.answer: In Bedrock, skeleton horses can be controlled while riding without a saddle.

fire.answer: Without protection, ordinary fire and lava can damage it. Being undead, large, or adapted to a particular biome does not by itself grant fire immunity.

variants.answer: A skeleton trap horse and a triggered horse with a skeleton rider have different encounter states. Horse and rider remain separate mobs.

spawn_conditions.answer: Natural skeleton trap horses are associated with thunderstorm lightning. Channeling-trident lightning and lightning directed to a lightning rod do not produce traps. A normal horse struck by lightning is not the recipe for a skeleton horse.

leashing.answer: Yes. Use a lead on it to move it, then use a fence to tie it there. You can remove the lead with shears. Leashing does not tame the creature or give it immunity to hazards.

experience.answer: An adult can drop 1–3 experience points after a player or tamed-wolf kill. Babies do not give death experience. These are experience points, not player levels.

experience_baby.answer: The baby does not give experience when killed. Growing into an adult changes its death reward; it is separate from experience earned by successful breeding.

lifetime.answer: An untriggered skeleton trap horse has a 15-minute timer even if named. Triggering the trap is a different state; the resulting horses and riders have their own persistence. Do not assume naming an untriggered trap freezes its timer.

growth.answer: Skeleton horses cannot breed, so they have no normal breeding-and-raising cycle. I do not have a growth time to give you for a command-created baby.

relocation.answer: You can use a lead to move a skeleton horse. Guide it along a safe route, keep it close enough that the lead does not break, and protect it from falls and unsuitable water or heat.

attack_style.answer: A skeleton horse itself does not attack players. The skeleton horseman attacks through its separate skeleton rider.

provocation.answer: Triggering a skeleton trap creates a dangerous mounted encounter, but the horse and rider have separate roles. A riderless skeleton horse is passive.

counterplay.answer: Deal with the skeleton rider while avoiding unnecessary damage to the horse if you want to keep it. Do not expect feeding to breed a replacement skeleton horse.

identity.answer: A skeleton horse is an undead rideable horse. Certain skeleton-trap encounters can produce them. It is not an ordinary breedable horse.

behavior.answer: A skeleton horse is an undead rideable horse. Certain skeleton-trap encounters can produce them. It is not an ordinary breedable horse.

health.answer: Its normal maximum health is 15 health points (7.5 hearts). Effects can change its health during play.

water.answer: It can breathe underwater.

spawning.answer: Look below Y=40 in a slime chunk, or in swamps and mangrove swamps at Y=51–69 with light level 7 or less. Swamp spawning depends on the moon: full moons are best, and new moons produce none. In Bedrock, slime-chunk coordinates are the same across world seeds.

drops.answer: The smallest slimes can drop slimeballs. Larger slimes split into smaller ones, so finish the smaller sizes to collect their slimeball drops. The total yield depends on how many children appear and the loot conditions.

health.answer: Normal large slimes have 16 health points, medium slimes have 4 and small slimes have 1. Special sizes can have different values.

combat.answer: Larger slimes hurt you by contact and split when killed. Small slimes do not deal normal contact damage, but can still push or distract you.

taming.answer: Slime cannot be tamed as player-owned pets.

breeding.answer: You cannot breed a slime. Larger ones split into smaller ones when killed; that is not food-based breeding.

sunlight.answer: Sunlight alone does not make it burn like an exposed zombie or skeleton. Other hazards, such as being out of water or changing dimensions, can still matter for the species.

fire.answer: Without protection, ordinary fire and lava can damage it. Being undead, large, or adapted to a particular biome does not by itself grant fire immunity.

variants.answer: Slimes have small, medium and large forms. Larger slimes split when killed; only the smallest size normally drops slimeballs.

water.answer: Slimes can swim but can drown when submerged for too long. Larger slimes can split into smaller slimes when they die.

spawn_conditions.answer: Underground slime-chunk spawning needs Y below 40 and does not depend on light or weather. Swamp spawning needs Y=51–69, light level 7 or less and a suitable moon phase; none spawn there on a new moon. Leave clear space. In Bedrock, slime-chunk coordinates are the same across world seeds.

experience.answer: Small, medium and large cubes give 1, 2 and 4 experience points respectively after a qualifying player kill. Those values are per cube killed, not a combined total for every smaller cube that might split from it.

attack_style.answer: Larger slimes hop into targets and split into smaller slimes when killed. The smallest slimes cannot damage players.

provocation.answer: Slimes are hostile mobs, but their danger depends on size. Killing a large slime can leave more moving targets instead of ending the encounter.

counterplay.answer: Leave room to deal with split offspring. Do not treat the original large slime’s death as proof that every smaller slime is gone.

growth.answer: Small slimes are size variants, not growing babies. They do not become larger just by waiting or feeding; larger slimes split into smaller ones when killed.

lifetime.answer: A naturally spawned slime can disappear through ordinary distance despawning unless it has become persistent. In Bedrock, a name tag is one way to prevent ordinary distance despawning; distance rules depend on simulation settings and mob state. A boat or minecart alone is not a blanket persistence guarantee, and persistence does not prevent death.

relocation.answer: A minecart can carry a slime in Bedrock. Bring an empty cart into contact with it, then use rails and powered rails along a protected route. An active activator rail can eject the passenger. It can still be dangerous while riding; a cart is not taming or protection from its attacks. The cart alone does not guarantee persistence in Bedrock.

identity.answer: A slime is a bouncing hostile mob that divides into smaller slimes when killed. Its smaller forms can provide slimeballs used for sticky pistons and other recipes.

behavior.answer: A slime is a bouncing hostile mob that divides into smaller slimes when killed. Its smaller forms can provide slimeballs used for sticky pistons and other recipes.

identity.answer: This is the small slime size.

health.answer: This size has 1 health points.

drops.answer: Small slimes provide slimeballs. Larger slimes split into smaller slimes when killed.

identity.answer: This is the medium slime size.

health.answer: This size has 4 health points.

drops.answer: Small slimes provide slimeballs. Larger slimes split into smaller slimes when killed.

identity.answer: This is the large slime size.

health.answer: This size has 16 health points.

drops.answer: Small slimes provide slimeballs. Larger slimes split into smaller slimes when killed.

spawning.answer: Blazes shoot small fireballs, and dispensers launch them from fire charges.

combat.answer: Small fireballs can ignite targets and blocks. They are not the same explosive, deflectable projectile as a ghast fireball.

projectile_use.answer: Blazes and certain other sources fire small fireballs. They are not the large explosive ghast fireball.

projectile_effects.answer: A small fireball can deal damage and ignite a target. A shield can block a blaze fireball’s damage and ignition.

retrieval.answer: Do not try to return a blaze’s small fireball using the large-ghast-fireball method. Avoid it or block it rather than expecting a recoverable item.

identity.answer: A small fireball is a fiery projectile used by mobs such as blazes. It can burn targets and ignite suitable surfaces, so use cover rather than trying to collect it.

behavior.answer: A small fireball is a fiery projectile used by mobs such as blazes. It can burn targets and ignite suitable surfaces, so use cover rather than trying to collect it.

spawning.answer: Brush suspicious sand in warm ocean ruins to look for sniffer eggs, then hatch an egg. Sniffers do not naturally spawn as wandering adults.

drops.answer: Sniffers have no normal item drops on death. Torchflower seeds and pitcher pods are dug up by living adults; sniffer eggs come from breeding.

breeding.answer: Bedrock sniffers must be at full health to breed. Use torchflower seeds on two adults; successful breeding drops a sniffer egg and starts a five-minute breeding cooldown.

interactions.answer: Adult sniffers dig torchflower seeds and pitcher pods from suitable ground after a cooldown. They cannot dig every block; mycelium does not work.

taming.answer: Sniffer cannot be tamed as player-owned pets. You can still ask how to breed them.

fire.answer: Without protection, it can take fire and lava damage and die. Living in a warm biome or having a particular coat color does not grant fire immunity.

sunlight.answer: Ordinary sunlight does not make this creature spontaneously burn. Fire, lava and lightning are separate hazards.

water.answer: It needs air and can drown if trapped fully underwater. Being able to swim or float is not the same as being able to breathe underwater.

powder_snow.answer: It can take freezing damage while trapped in powder snow without applicable protection. A cold-biome home or white coat alone does not guarantee freezing immunity.

hatching.answer: Place a sniffer egg to hatch it. It normally takes about 20 minutes, or about 10 minutes on moss. An egg item sitting loose in an inventory does not hatch.

digging.answer: An adult sniffer needs reachable diggable ground beneath its head. It cannot dig while leashed, in water, tempted by a torchflower seed, panicking or riding in a boat or minecart. After digging, it waits eight minutes and avoids its previous 20 digging spots. It finds torchflower seeds or pitcher pods, not ores.

land.answer: It can live on land. Still provide suitable safe terrain and protect it from fire, falls or other species-specific hazards.

age_lock.answer: Use a golden dandelion on an eligible baby to pause its aging. Use another golden dandelion on that same baby to resume aging. This is separate from feeding normal food to speed growth.

variants.answer: A baby sniffer is called a snifflet. A sniffer egg is a separate block that hatches into a snifflet.

spawn_conditions.answer: A sniffer must hatch from an egg; breeding existing sniffers can also produce eggs. For the first egg, use archaeology in warm ocean ruins. Waiting in a biome or building a dark platform does not make adult sniffers naturally appear.

leashing.answer: Yes. Use a lead on it to move it, then use a fence to tie it there. You can remove the lead with shears. Leashing does not tame the creature or give it immunity to hazards.

breeding_conditions.answer: Bedrock sniffers must be at full health to breed. Use torchflower seeds on two adults; successful breeding drops a sniffer egg and starts a five-minute breeding cooldown.

experience.answer: An adult can drop 1–3 experience points after a player or tamed-wolf kill. Babies do not give death experience. These are experience points, not player levels.

experience_baby.answer: The baby does not give experience when killed. Growing into an adult changes its death reward; it is separate from experience earned by successful breeding.

experience_breeding.answer: Successful breeding gives 1–7 experience points. That reward comes from breeding, not from killing the baby. The animal’s own breeding requirements still apply.

relocation.answer: You can lead a sniffer, but it cannot dig while leashed. Set up safe, reachable diggable ground at the destination and release the lead before expecting seed digging.

breeding_age.answer: No. A baby cannot breed; it must grow into an adult first. Food that helps it grow is not the same as breeding food being used on an adult.

breeding_health.answer: Both adult sniffers must be at full health before breeding. In Bedrock, torchflower seeds can heal them; breeding food does not skip the health requirement.

digging_age.answer: A snifflet cannot dig up ancient seeds. Let it grow into an adult, then provide suitable reachable ground and meet its other digging requirements.

growth.answer: A snifflet normally takes about 40 minutes of active game time to become an adult sniffer. Egg hatching is a separate timer. You can speed this up by feeding it torchflower seeds.

diet.answer: Torchflower seeds breed adult sniffers and help snifflets grow. In Bedrock they can also heal sniffers. Sniffers need full health for breeding, and snifflets must grow up before they can dig for seeds.

lifetime.answer: Sniffers normally have persistence in Bedrock and do not disappear through ordinary distance despawning. They can still be killed or removed by other game rules.

attack_style.answer: Sniffers do not attack players or act as combat pets. Their main activity is searching suitable ground and digging for ancient plants.

provocation.answer: Disturbing a sniffer does not trigger hostile retaliation. A snifflet cannot dig until it grows up, but that age difference does not make it aggressive.

counterplay.answer: Protect sniffers from hazards and provide suitable digging space. Use torchflower seeds for their feeding interactions instead of fighting them.

identity.answer: A sniffer is an ancient passive animal hatched from a sniffer egg. It digs up special ancient plant seeds or pods from suitable ground, helping players grow decorative plants.

behavior.answer: A sniffer is an ancient passive animal hatched from a sniffer egg. It digs up special ancient plant seeds or pods from suitable ground, helping players grow decorative plants.

combat.answer: It does not normally attack players. It digs up special ancient plant seeds or pods from suitable ground, helping players grow decorative plants.

health.answer: Its normal maximum health is 14 health points (7 hearts). Effects can change its health during play.

spawning.answer: Snow golems are constructed rather than naturally spawning as ordinary wildlife.

construction.answer: Stack two snow blocks and place a carved pumpkin or jack o’lantern on top last. Leave enough room for the resulting snow golem.

drops.answer: Snow golems can drop snowballs on death. Shearing a living golem removes its carved pumpkin; that is a separate interaction.

combat.answer: Snow golems throw snowballs at hostile targets, but most mobs do not take direct damage from ordinary snowballs. Blazes are an important exception.

interactions.answer: Snow golems can leave a snow trail where the environment allows it. Rain, water and hot surroundings can harm them. Shears remove the pumpkin head.

taming.answer: Snow golem cannot be tamed as player-owned pets.

breeding.answer: You cannot breed a snow golem. They are created using their construction or summoning method instead.

water.answer: Water damages snow golems. Do not use a water-filled enclosure to keep one.

rain.answer: Rain damages exposed snow golems. Provide overhead shelter if the biome can rain.

powder_snow.answer: Snow golems are immune to ordinary powder-snow freezing damage.

shearing.answer: Use shears to remove its pumpkin covering. This exposes its face without making it a different kind of golem.

temperature.answer: Hot biomes can damage snow golems. Bedrock also restricts their snow trails in warm biomes; snow-trail rules and heat damage are separate conditions.

fire.answer: Without protection, ordinary fire and lava can damage it. Being undead, large, or adapted to a particular biome does not by itself grant fire immunity.

sunlight.answer: Sunlight itself does not ignite a snow golem like a zombie. Hot-biome damage can still hurt it, and rain or water are separate hazards.

variants.answer: A snow golem can wear its carved-pumpkin head or have it removed with shears to reveal its face. This does not create a new species.

spawn_conditions.answer: Create one using two snow blocks and a carved pumpkin or jack o’lantern, with the pumpkin placed last. Ordinary snow layers or an uncarved pumpkin do not substitute. It does not naturally spawn just because the biome is snowy.

leashing.answer: Yes. Use a lead on it to move it, then use a fence to tie it there. You can remove the lead with shears. Leashing does not tame the creature or give it immunity to hazards.

experience.answer: It gives no experience when killed. Item drops and rewards from other interactions are separate.

attack_style.answer: Snow golems throw snowballs at monsters. The snowballs normally cause knockback without health damage, but they deal damage to blazes.

provocation.answer: Snow golems do not intentionally attack players. They provoke monsters by throwing snowballs, which can cause those monsters to attack the golem.

counterplay.answer: Protect a snow golem from retaliation and do not rely on it to kill ordinary monsters. Shelter it from water, rain and damaging heat; its snowballs are a distraction rather than a replacement for secure defenses.

growth.answer: A snow golem has no normal baby form that grows into an adult. There is no ordinary baby-growth timer or growth food to use for this mob.

lifetime.answer: Snow Golems normally have persistence in Bedrock and do not disappear through ordinary distance despawning. They can still be killed or removed by other game rules.

relocation.answer: You can use a lead to move a snow golem. Guide it along a safe route, keep it close enough that the lead does not break, and protect it from falls and unsuitable water or heat.

identity.answer: A snow golem is a player-built mob made using snow blocks and a carved pumpkin or suitable equivalent. It throws snowballs at many hostile mobs and can leave snow trails in suitable conditions. Heat and water can harm it.

behavior.answer: A snow golem is a player-built mob made using snow blocks and a carved pumpkin or suitable equivalent. It throws snowballs at many hostile mobs and can leave snow trails in suitable conditions. Heat and water can harm it.

health.answer: Its normal maximum health is 4 health points (2 hearts). Effects can change its health during play.

fall_damage.answer: It does not take ordinary fall damage. Other damage sources can still hurt it.

identity.answer: This snow golem has had its pumpkin covering removed.

shearing.answer: Use shears to remove the pumpkin covering. This does not turn it into a different species or change its ordinary snow-golem hazards.

spawning.answer: Throw a snowball or fire one from a dispenser. Snow golems also throw snowballs.

combat.answer: Snowballs push or provoke many targets without normal weapon damage, but they can damage blazes. They are not a substitute for a weapon against every hostile mob.

projectile_use.answer: Throw snowballs as projectiles. Snow golems also throw their own snowball projectiles.

projectile_effects.answer: Snowballs deal three health points of damage to blazes, but do not deal ordinary damage to other mobs. They can still cause knockback and provoke retaliation.

retrieval.answer: Thrown snowballs are not arrows that lodge in blocks for recovery. Collect new snowballs rather than expecting to retrieve each throw.

identity.answer: A snowball is a throwable item and projectile. Throw it to knock or distract suitable targets; it also has special interactions with some mobs, including blazes.

behavior.answer: A snowball is a throwable item and projectile. Throw it to knock or distract suitable targets; it also has special interactions with some mobs, including blazes.

spawning.answer: Spiders appear in suitable dark Overworld locations, and from certain monster or trial spawners. They need more horizontal room than many humanoid mobs.

drops.answer: Spiders can drop string, and a player kill can also produce a spider eye. Looting affects the applicable drops.

combat.answer: Spiders climb walls and can become hostile in darkness or after being attacked. Bright light affects their normal aggression. Cave spiders are smaller and have different poison behavior.

taming.answer: Spider cannot be tamed as player-owned pets.

breeding.answer: You cannot breed a spider.

sunlight.answer: Sunlight alone does not make it burn like an exposed zombie or skeleton. Other hazards, such as being out of water or changing dimensions, can still matter for the species.

fire.answer: Without protection, ordinary fire and lava can damage it. Being undead, large, or adapted to a particular biome does not by itself grant fire immunity.

variants.answer: Regular spiders and cave spiders are different mobs. A spider jockey has a separate skeleton rider, not a new baby-spider form.

spawn_conditions.answer: Natural spiders need a suitable dark surface and enough clear width. Bedrock excludes mushroom fields, deep dark, rivers, frozen rivers and snowy plains; sulfur caves replace ordinary spider spawns with cave spiders. Spawner encounters are a separate route.

experience.answer: It gives 5 experience points after a player or tamed-wolf kill. Looting affects certain item drops, not this experience reward.

attack_style.answer: A spider closes the distance, jumps and bites. It can climb walls, so a simple vertical barrier may not stop it.

provocation.answer: Spiders attack on sight in dark conditions and are normally neutral in bright conditions unless provoked. Bright surroundings do not make an already hostile encounter automatically safe.

counterplay.answer: Use barriers with space and overhangs rather than assuming a plain wall stops it. Avoid provoking a neutral spider while dealing with other threats.

growth.answer: A spider has no normal baby form that grows into an adult. There is no ordinary baby-growth timer or growth food to use for this mob.

lifetime.answer: A naturally spawned spider can disappear through ordinary distance despawning unless it has become persistent. In Bedrock, a name tag is one way to prevent ordinary distance despawning; distance rules depend on simulation settings and mob state. A boat or minecart alone is not a blanket persistence guarantee, and persistence does not prevent death.

relocation.answer: A minecart can carry a spider in Bedrock. Bring an empty cart into contact with it, then use rails and powered rails along a protected route. An active activator rail can eject the passenger. It can still be dangerous while riding; a cart is not taming or protection from its attacks. The cart alone does not guarantee persistence in Bedrock.

identity.answer: A spider is a climbing mob that can become hostile depending on conditions. It climbs walls and attacks at close range. Brightness affects its ordinary aggression.

behavior.answer: A spider is a climbing mob that can become hostile depending on conditions. It climbs walls and attacks at close range. Brightness affects its ordinary aggression.

health.answer: Its normal maximum health is 16 health points (8 hearts). Effects can change its health during play.

spawning.answer: Throw a splash potion or launch it with a dispenser to create the projectile.

interactions.answer: A splash potion breaks on impact and applies its effect nearby. The effect depends on the potion, and distance can affect its strength or duration.

projectile_use.answer: Throw it so its splash reaches the intended target. A direct hit can apply a stronger or longer result than being near the edge.

projectile_effects.answer: Its effect depends on the potion. Healing and Harming interact differently with undead targets; do not assume every healing potion heals every mob.

retrieval.answer: The thrown bottle is consumed rather than returning as a reusable glass bottle.

identity.answer: A splash potion is a throwable potion. Throw it to apply its effect around the impact point; the effect depends on the potion's contents.

behavior.answer: A splash potion is a throwable potion. Throw it to apply its effect around the impact point; the effect depends on the potion's contents.

spawning.answer: Look in ocean and river water. Bedrock squid are surface water spawns rather than underground cave spawns.

drops.answer: Squid can drop 1–3 ink sacs, with Looting increasing applicable amounts. Ordinary squid do not drop glow ink sacs.

breeding.answer: Squid cannot be bred.

taming.answer: Squid cannot be tamed.

age_lock.answer: Use a golden dandelion on an eligible baby to pause its aging. Use another golden dandelion on that same baby to resume aging. This is separate from feeding normal food to speed growth.

variants.answer: Squid have baby and adult stages and cannot be bred with food. Glow squid are a different species.

growth.answer: A baby squid normally takes about 20 minutes of active game time to become an adult. Feeding does not speed up its growth. Keep it in water while you wait.

spawn_conditions.answer: A Bedrock squid spawn must not have a solid or spawnable block above the location. Do not assume all squid need the same height range as ocean fish. A roofed tank can fail even though it contains water.

leashing.answer: Yes. Use a lead on it to move it, then use a fence to tie it there. You can remove the lead with shears. Leashing does not tame the creature or give it immunity to hazards.

experience.answer: An adult gives 1–3 experience points after a player or tamed-wolf kill. Baby squid give no death experience.

experience_baby.answer: Baby squid give no experience when killed.

lifetime.answer: A naturally spawned squid can disappear through ordinary distance despawning unless it has become persistent. In Bedrock, a name tag is one way to prevent ordinary distance despawning; distance rules depend on simulation settings and mob state. A boat or minecart alone is not a blanket persistence guarantee, and persistence does not prevent death.

relocation.answer: You can use a lead to move a squid. Guide it along a safe route, keep it close enough that the lead does not break, and protect it from falls and unsuitable water or heat. Keep it in water: it cannot survive an ordinary dry-land walk.

attack_style.answer: Squid do not attack players or shoot damaging ink attacks. They are passive aquatic mobs.

provocation.answer: A squid does not become hostile when disturbed. An ink effect is a defensive visual response, not a damaging projectile.

counterplay.answer: Keep it in water if preserving it; it needs water to breathe. No combat protection from a squid is normally needed.

identity.answer: A squid is a passive aquatic animal. It provides ink sacs when killed; it is not a tameable riding animal.

behavior.answer: A squid is a passive aquatic animal. It provides ink sacs when killed; it is not a tameable riding animal.

combat.answer: It does not normally attack players. It provides ink sacs when killed; it is not a tameable riding animal.

health.answer: Its normal maximum health is 10 health points (5 hearts). Effects can change its health during play.

water.answer: It can breathe underwater. It cannot breathe air normally, so keep it in water.

land.answer: It needs water to breathe normally. Keeping it out of water can cause suffocation damage.

spawning.answer: Strays replace some skeleton spawns in snowy biomes. Bedrock includes frozen rivers, frozen oceans and certain snowy mountain biomes. Ordinary skeletons can also become strays after remaining in powder snow.

drops.answer: Strays can drop bones, arrows and, under suitable player-kill conditions, an arrow of Slowness. Carried equipment has separate rules.

combat.answer: Strays shoot arrows that inflict Slowness. They are undead ranged attackers, so cover and a shield are useful.

interactions.answer: Powder snow can convert an ordinary skeleton into a stray. Bogged and parched do not use that same conversion rule.

taming.answer: Stray cannot be tamed as player-owned pets.

breeding.answer: You cannot breed a stray.

powder_snow.answer: Strays are immune to ordinary powder-snow freezing damage. A normal skeleton can convert to a stray in powder snow.

fire.answer: Without protection, ordinary fire and lava can damage it. Being undead, large, or adapted to a particular biome does not by itself grant fire immunity.

variants.answer: A stray is a cold-biome skeleton-type mob. It is distinct from a wither skeleton, bogged and parched.

spawn_conditions.answer: Strays naturally occur in eligible snowy and frozen biomes. Another route is keeping an ordinary skeleton in powder snow until it converts; bogged and parched do not use that conversion. Certain trial spawners can also spawn strays.

experience.answer: The base reward is 5 experience points after a player or tamed-wolf kill. Naturally spawned equipment can affect the total; picked-up equipment and whether the gear itself drops are separate conditions. Looting does not multiply experience.

equipment_drops.answer: Naturally spawned weapons or armor are not guaranteed drops. Qualifying player or tamed-wolf kills and Looting can matter. Equipment the mob picked up later is a different category; do not assume one chance covers both. Its ordinary body loot is separate.

attack_style.answer: A stray fires arrows that can apply Slowness, making it harder to escape.

provocation.answer: Strays are hostile skeleton-type mobs and can attack without being hit first.

counterplay.answer: Use cover and block arrows. Watch your movement when slowed, particularly near ledges or other hostile mobs.

growth.answer: A stray has no normal baby form that grows into an adult. There is no ordinary baby-growth timer or growth food to use for this mob.

lifetime.answer: A naturally spawned stray can disappear through ordinary distance despawning unless it has become persistent. In Bedrock, a name tag is one way to prevent ordinary distance despawning; distance rules depend on simulation settings and mob state. A boat or minecart alone is not a blanket persistence guarantee, and persistence does not prevent death.

relocation.answer: A minecart can carry a stray in Bedrock. Bring an empty cart into contact with it, then use rails and powered rails along a protected route. An active activator rail can eject the passenger. It can still be dangerous while riding; a cart is not taming or protection from its attacks. The cart alone does not guarantee persistence in Bedrock.

identity.answer: A stray is a cold-region skeleton variant. It fires arrows that inflict Slowness, making it harder to escape follow-up attacks.

behavior.answer: A stray is a cold-region skeleton variant. It fires arrows that inflict Slowness, making it harder to escape follow-up attacks.

health.answer: Its normal maximum health is 20 health points (10 hearts). Effects can change its health during play.

sunlight.answer: It can burn in direct sunlight when unprotected. Shade, water and applicable armor protection can prevent that; sunlight protection does not make it immune to lava.

water.answer: It can breathe underwater.

spawning.answer: Striders naturally appear on lava in every Nether biome where their spawning conditions are met.

drops.answer: Adult striders drop 2–5 string and any equipped saddle. In Bedrock, their string drop is not increased by Looting.

breeding.answer: Feed warped fungus to two adult striders.

taming.answer: Striders do not require taming. Equip a saddle to ride one, then use a warped fungus on a stick to steer.

transport.answer: Ride a saddled strider across lava using a warped fungus on a stick. It slows down when cold and out of lava; water is dangerous to it.

water.answer: Water and rain can hurt striders. Keep a strider on lava or suitable dry terrain rather than treating it as a normal water mount.

rain.answer: Rain can damage an exposed strider.

powder_snow.answer: Striders take extra freezing damage in powder snow despite being fire-immune.

temperature.answer: Striders stay warm on lava. Away from suitable warmth they shiver, become purple and move more slowly; this is a state change, not a new species.

equipment.answer: A saddle allows riding, and a warped fungus on a stick controls the strider. Ordinary warped fungus is its breeding food, not the same thing as the control item.

age_lock.answer: Use a golden dandelion on an eligible baby to pause its aging. Use another golden dandelion on that same baby to resume aging. This is separate from feeding normal food to speed growth.

variants.answer: Striders have baby and adult stages. Their warm red and cold purple appearances reflect temperature, not separate breeds.

spawn_conditions.answer: Striders naturally spawn on lava with air above in Nether biomes. A dry platform does not provide their usual spawning medium. In Bedrock their animal population cap is shared with hoglins, so other animals can affect availability.

leashing.answer: Yes. Use a lead on it to move it, then use a fence to tie it there. You can remove the lead with shears. Leashing does not tame the creature or give it immunity to hazards.

experience.answer: An adult can drop 1–3 experience points after a player or tamed-wolf kill. Babies do not give death experience. These are experience points, not player levels.

experience_baby.answer: The baby does not give experience when killed. Growing into an adult changes its death reward; it is separate from experience earned by successful breeding.

experience_breeding.answer: Successful breeding gives 1–7 experience points. That reward comes from breeding, not from killing the baby. The animal’s own breeding requirements still apply.

relocation.answer: Use a saddle and warped fungus on a stick to control it, or guide it with a lead. Lava travel suits a strider; bringing it into water or rain is dangerous.

breeding_age.answer: No. A baby cannot breed; it must grow into an adult first. Food that helps it grow is not the same as breeding food being used on an adult.

growth.answer: A baby strider normally takes about 20 minutes of active game time to become an adult. You can speed this up by feeding it warped fungus.

diet.answer: Warped fungus breeds adult striders and helps babies grow. For riding, use a saddle and steer with warped fungus on a stick; feeding plain warped fungus is a different interaction.

lifetime.answer: A naturally spawned strider can disappear through ordinary distance despawning unless it has become persistent. In Bedrock, a name tag is one way to prevent ordinary distance despawning; distance rules depend on simulation settings and mob state. Suitable player interactions, such as breeding, tempting with accepted food or leashing where supported, can also give persistence. A boat or minecart alone is not a blanket persistence guarantee, and persistence does not prevent death.

attack_style.answer: Striders do not attack players. Their ability to walk on lava does not make their riders immune to lava.

provocation.answer: A strider stays passive when handled; shivering away from lava is a temperature response, not anger.

counterplay.answer: Use a saddle and warped fungus on a stick to ride it. Keep yourself clear of lava when mounting or dismounting rather than relying on the strider as protection.

identity.answer: A strider is a passive Nether animal that walks on lava. Saddle it and steer with a warped fungus on a stick for lava travel. It becomes cold and slower away from lava.

behavior.answer: A strider is a passive Nether animal that walks on lava. Saddle it and steer with a warped fungus on a stick for lava travel. It becomes cold and slower away from lava.

combat.answer: It does not normally attack players. Saddle it and steer with a warped fungus on a stick for lava travel. It becomes cold and slower away from lava.

health.answer: Its normal maximum health is 20 health points (10 hearts). Effects can change its health during play.

fire.answer: It is immune to ordinary fire and lava damage. That does not protect it from every other kind of damage.

sunlight.answer: Ordinary sunlight does not make it take burning damage. It is fire-immune, although other environmental hazards can still matter.

identity.answer: A cold strider is shivering outside warm conditions.

spawning.answer: A strider becomes cold away from lava; purple is a temperature state rather than a separate biome-specific species.

interactions.answer: Return it to lava or suitable warmth. A cold strider moves more slowly.

spawning.answer: Look in sulfur caves, where large sulfur cubes naturally spawn at any light level.

health.answer: Large sulfur cubes have 8 health points and small sulfur cubes have 4.

drops.answer: A large sulfur cube drops the block it absorbed when it dies. Small cubes do not provide the same experience drop.

interactions.answer: Sulfur cubes can absorb supported blocks, changing their properties. Use shears to remove an absorbed block. A dangerous absorbed block, such as TNT or magma, can make an otherwise passive cube hazardous.

taming.answer: Sulfur cube cannot be tamed as player-owned pets.

breeding.answer: Sulfur cubes do not breed by pairing adults with food. When a large sulfur cube dies without exploding, it splits into two small cubes; those can grow into large ones.

sunlight.answer: Sunlight alone does not make it burn like an exposed zombie or skeleton. Other hazards, such as being out of water or changing dimensions, can still matter for the species.

water.answer: A sulfur cube’s block-carrying state changes its breathing rules. A block-carrying form can breathe underwater; do not assume every size or empty form has identical environmental protection.

fire.answer: A block-carrying sulfur cube can be primed by fire-related damage. Do not treat its many damage protections as general fire or lava immunity.

age_lock.answer: Use a golden dandelion on an eligible baby to pause its aging. Use another golden dandelion on that same baby to resume aging. This is separate from feeding normal food to speed growth.

variants.answer: Sulfur cubes can have different sizes and can carry a block. Their block-carrying state is not an animal coat breed.

spawn_conditions.answer: Check the sulfur-caves biome and a suitable clear spawning space. Darkness is not required. Small sulfur cubes come from a large cube splitting and can grow; they are not the ordinary naturally spawned form.

leashing.answer: Yes. Use a lead on it to move it, then use a fence to tie it there. You can remove the lead with shears. Leashing does not tame the creature or give it immunity to hazards.

bucketing.answer: Use an empty bucket on a large sulfur cube. Small sulfur cubes cannot be bucketed. A cube with ignited TNT also cannot be captured. A carried block is retained in the bucket; this is different from aquatic mobs needing water buckets.

experience.answer: A large sulfur cube can give 1–2 experience points after a player kill. Small sulfur cubes give no experience; a block it was carrying is a separate item drop.

experience_baby.answer: Small sulfur cubes give no experience when killed; the large form has a different reward.

lifetime.answer: A large sulfur cube that has been bucketed and released does not ordinarily despawn. If it splits, the resulting small cubes can despawn; do not assume the parent’s bucket history preserves every offspring.

relocation.answer: Use an empty bucket on a large sulfur cube for compact transport. Small cubes and cubes carrying ignited TNT cannot be captured. This uses an empty bucket, unlike aquatic creatures needing water buckets.

growth.answer: A small sulfur cube normally takes about 20 minutes of active game time to grow into a large sulfur cube. You can speed this up by feeding it slimeballs.

diet.answer: Feed slimeballs to a small sulfur cube to help it grow into a large one. Large sulfur cubes can absorb blocks, but absorbing a block is different from eating a slimeball or breeding a pair of animals.

attack_style.answer: Sulfur cubes are normally passive, but an absorbed block can create hazards, including damaging magma contact or an ignited explosive form.

provocation.answer: A sulfur cube is not an ordinary hostile slime. The block it absorbs changes its behavior, so passive behavior does not make every configuration safe.

counterplay.answer: Check the absorbed block before approaching. Keep explosive forms away from buildings, and distinguish passive movement from block-based damage.

identity.answer: A sulfur cube is a cube-shaped animal that can carry a suitable block. The block it holds can change its movement and other behavior. Some interactions can make it dangerous, including explosive behavior.

behavior.answer: A sulfur cube is a cube-shaped animal that can carry a suitable block. The block it holds can change its movement and other behavior. Some interactions can make it dangerous, including explosive behavior.

combat.answer: It does not normally attack players. The block it holds can change its movement and other behavior. Some interactions can make it dangerous, including explosive behavior.

spawning.answer: Tadpoles hatch from frogspawn laid by breeding frogs. They are the growing stage that becomes a frog.

drops.answer: Tadpoles do not drop items or experience when killed.

breeding.answer: Tadpoles cannot breed; grow them into adult frogs first, then breed the frogs with slimeballs.

interactions.answer: Use a water bucket to move a tadpole and slimeballs to accelerate its growth. The biome where it matures determines the frog variant; its parents’ colors do not force the result.

taming.answer: Tadpole cannot be tamed as player-owned pets.

hatching.answer: Frogspawn hatches into tadpoles in water. Carry a tadpole in a water bucket; the biome where it grows up determines whether its frog form is temperate, warm or cold.

sunlight.answer: Sunlight alone does not make it burn like an exposed zombie or skeleton. Other hazards, such as being out of water or changing dimensions, can still matter for the species.

fire.answer: Without protection, ordinary fire and lava can damage it. Being undead, large, or adapted to a particular biome does not by itself grant fire immunity.

age_lock.answer: Use a golden dandelion on an eligible baby to pause its aging. Use another golden dandelion on that same baby to resume aging. This is separate from feeding normal food to speed growth.

variants.answer: A tadpole is a young frog. The biome where it grows up determines the resulting frog color.

spawn_conditions.answer: Tadpoles hatch from frogspawn laid by breeding frogs. A pond without frogspawn does not spontaneously produce tadpoles, and their eventual frog color depends on where they grow up.

leashing.answer: No, you cannot attach an ordinary lead to it through normal player interaction.

bucketing.answer: Use a water bucket on a tadpole to move it. Its age, health and name are preserved. After release it can still grow into a frog, whose color depends on the growth biome. A dispenser can release it but cannot capture it.

experience.answer: It gives no experience when killed. Item drops and rewards from other interactions are separate.

lifetime.answer: Catching it in a water bucket and releasing it prevents ordinary natural despawning. That does not prevent damage or death. A tadpole can still grow into a frog; capture is not a command to stop aging.

relocation.answer: Capture it with a water bucket, carry the filled bucket, and release it into safe water at the destination. Protect aquatic creatures from dry land. A dispenser can release a filled bucket but cannot catch a creature with a water bucket.

growth.answer: A tadpole normally takes about 20 minutes of active game time to become a frog. The biome where it grows up determines its frog variant. You can speed this up by feeding it slimeballs.

diet.answer: Feed slimeballs to a tadpole to help it grow into a frog. The biome where it grows up determines its frog variant; feeding does not make it breed while it is still a tadpole.

attack_style.answer: Tadpoles do not attack players. They are the passive aquatic young stage of frogs.

provocation.answer: A tadpole does not retaliate against players. Out-of-water danger is a survival problem, not aggression.

counterplay.answer: Use a water bucket to move it, and keep it in water until it grows into a frog. Protect it from axolotls and other hazards.

identity.answer: A tadpole is the young aquatic stage of a frog. Carry it in a water bucket and raise it into a frog. Its growing environment affects which frog variant it becomes.

behavior.answer: A tadpole is the young aquatic stage of a frog. Carry it in a water bucket and raise it into a frog. Its growing environment affects which frog variant it becomes.

combat.answer: It does not normally attack players. Carry it in a water bucket and raise it into a frog. Its growing environment affects which frog variant it becomes.

health.answer: Its normal maximum health is 6 health points (3 hearts). Effects can change its health during play.

water.answer: It can breathe underwater. It cannot breathe air normally, so keep it in water.

land.answer: It needs water to breathe normally. Keeping it out of water can cause suffocation damage.

spawning.answer: Throw a trident to create its projectile; some drowned also throw tridents.

interactions.answer: A player’s thrown trident can be recovered, and Loyalty can return it. Channeling and Riptide have their own weather or water requirements. A drowned’s thrown projectile is not a freely recoverable player trident.

projectile_use.answer: Throw a trident as a projectile; a player’s trident is different from a drowned’s naturally held weapon.

projectile_effects.answer: A thrown trident damages targets. Loyalty returns it under suitable conditions, while Riptide is a different wet-weather movement enchantment and cannot be combined with Loyalty.

retrieval.answer: Thrown tridents do not ordinarily despawn in Bedrock. Pickup depends on ownership, enchantments and how it was thrown. You cannot collect every drowned-thrown trident just by walking over it.

identity.answer: A thrown trident is a trident travelling as a projectile. It deals damage on impact; recovery and return behavior depend on the trident and its enchantments.

behavior.answer: A thrown trident is a trident travelling as a projectile. It deals damage on impact; recovery and return behavior depend on the trident and its enchantments.

spawning.answer: Igniting TNT creates the primed TNT entity. Redstone, fire and other explosion-related triggers can ignite it.

interactions.answer: Primed TNT counts down and explodes, damaging nearby entities and breaking blocks. Water can protect blocks from much explosion damage without making nearby entities safe.

activation.answer: Redstone, fire and ignition sources can turn a TNT block into primed TNT. Once primed, it is a moving entity affected by gravity.

projectile_effects.answer: Ordinarily primed TNT explodes after its fuse. Water can prevent ordinary block destruction from the explosion, but nearby entities can still be hurt.

retrieval.answer: Primed TNT is not an item you can mine back into a safe TNT block. Avoid priming it near valuables or creatures you want to keep.

identity.answer: TNT is an explosive block that becomes a primed explosive entity when ignited. Use it for controlled explosions, keeping people, pets, and important builds well away from the blast.

behavior.answer: TNT is an explosive block that becomes a primed explosive entity when ignited. Use it for controlled explosions, keeping people, pets, and important builds well away from the blast.

spawning.answer: Place a crafted TNT minecart on rails.

interactions.answer: A powered activator rail can prime a TNT minecart. Other violent impacts or damage conditions can also trigger it, so keep it away from valuable builds.

drops.answer: Breaking an unprimed TNT minecart normally returns its item. An exploding TNT minecart is not a safe way to recover the cart.

storage.answer: A TNT minecart is an explosive rail vehicle, not a safe cargo chest or passenger seat.

propulsion.answer: A powered activator rail can prime it with a four-second fuse. Fire, damage and sufficiently hard falls can also cause dangerous activation.

retrieval.answer: Treat it as an explosive even when it looks like an ordinary cart. Do not use an assumed safe breaking method once it is primed or rely on another edition’s collision tricks.

identity.answer: A TNT minecart is an explosive rail vehicle. Certain activations and impacts can trigger it. Use it only where an explosion is intended.

behavior.answer: A TNT minecart is an explosive rail vehicle. Certain activations and impacts can trigger it. Use it only where an explosion is intended.

spawning.answer: Trader llamas arrive with wandering traders. They can also be produced by breeding suitable tamed trader llamas.

taming.answer: A trader llama still leashed to its wandering trader cannot be ridden normally. In Bedrock, detaching it from that trader makes it tamed and prevents normal trader-llama despawning.

breeding.answer: Feed hay bales to two tamed adult trader llamas. Their baby retains the trader-llama type and special rug.

transport.answer: Trader llamas can carry storage and form caravans. A rug is not a steering saddle; they are not controlled like horses.

drops.answer: Adult trader llamas can drop leather plus their applicable equipment and stored contents. Their lead is a separate item when detached.

health.answer: Trader llamas have a maximum health between 15 and 30 health points. Different individual llamas can have different maximum health.

variants.answer: Llamas have white, cream, gray and brown coats. Carpet color, trader decoration and chest storage are separate from the coat.

fire.answer: Without protection, it can take fire and lava damage and die. Living in a warm biome or having a particular coat color does not grant fire immunity.

sunlight.answer: Ordinary sunlight does not make this creature spontaneously burn. Fire, lava and lightning are separate hazards.

water.answer: It needs air and can drown if trapped fully underwater. Being able to swim or float is not the same as being able to breathe underwater.

powder_snow.answer: It can take freezing damage while trapped in powder snow without applicable protection. A cold-biome home or white coat alone does not guarantee freezing immunity.

storage.answer: A chest gives the llama storage based on its strength. Carpets decorate it but do not set its strength; llamas are not steered with a horse saddle.

equipment.answer: Llamas use carpets for decoration and chests for storage. Riding a llama does not make it steer like a saddled horse.

land.answer: It can live on land. Still provide suitable safe terrain and protect it from fire, falls or other species-specific hazards.

age_lock.answer: Use a golden dandelion on an eligible baby to pause its aging. Use another golden dandelion on that same baby to resume aging. This is separate from feeding normal food to speed growth.

spawn_conditions.answer: Two trader llamas attempt to appear with a wandering trader and are leashed to it. They are not a separately replenishing wild llama herd. Space around the trader matters to those attempts.

leashing.answer: Yes. Use a lead on it to move it, then use a fence to tie it there. You can remove the lead with shears. Leashing does not tame the creature or give it immunity to hazards.

experience.answer: An adult can drop 1–3 experience points after a player or tamed-wolf kill. Babies do not give death experience. These are experience points, not player levels.

experience_baby.answer: The baby does not give experience when killed. Growing into an adult changes its death reward; it is separate from experience earned by successful breeding.

experience_breeding.answer: Successful breeding gives 1–7 experience points. That reward comes from breeding, not from killing the baby. The animal’s own breeding requirements still apply.

lifetime.answer: A trader llama tied to a wandering trader can leave with the trader. In Bedrock, removing its lead from the trader makes it tamed and prevents that ordinary trader-linked despawn. Protect it from damage afterward.

breeding_age.answer: No. A baby cannot breed; it must grow into an adult first. Food that helps it grow is not the same as breeding food being used on an adult.

breeding_ownership.answer: The parents must be tamed before breeding. Use eligible adult animals and their breeding food; feeding wild animals is not enough to skip taming.

growth.answer: A baby trader llama normally takes about 20 minutes of active game time to become an adult. You can speed this up by feeding it wheat or hay bales.

diet.answer: Wheat and hay bales can heal trader llamas and help babies grow. Breeding needs tamed adults and hay bales, rather than wheat. Feeding does not by itself remove the wandering trader’s leash.

relocation.answer: You can use a lead to move a trader llama. Guide it along a safe route, keep it close enough that the lead does not break, and protect it from falls and unsuitable water or heat. A trader-owned llama may still be leashed to the wandering trader; deal with that leash before leading it elsewhere.

attack_style.answer: Trader llamas can spit at attackers. The wandering trader and each llama are separate entities.

provocation.answer: Attacking a trader llama or its wandering trader can provoke spitting. It is a neutral animal rather than a harmless decoration on the trader.

counterplay.answer: Avoid hitting the trader or llamas. Remove the trader’s leash before independent handling where needed; feeding or riding does not instantly make an ongoing attack safe.

identity.answer: A trader llama is a llama associated with a wandering trader. It carries the trader's decorations and can defend itself by spitting. It follows llama-style handling rules rather than villager trading rules.

behavior.answer: A trader llama is a llama associated with a wandering trader. It carries the trader's decorations and can defend itself by spitting. It follows llama-style handling rules rather than villager trading rules.

combat.answer: It can attack under particular conditions, so do not assume it is always harmless. It carries the trader's decorations and can defend itself by spitting. It follows llama-style handling rules rather than villager trading rules.

identity.answer: This is a white trader llama coat.

spawning.answer: Find trader llamas with wandering traders.

storage.answer: A llama’s strength controls its chest storage capacity; its coat color does not determine that strength.

identity.answer: This is a cream trader llama coat.

spawning.answer: Find trader llamas with wandering traders.

storage.answer: A llama’s strength controls its chest storage capacity; its coat color does not determine that strength.

identity.answer: This is a gray trader llama coat.

spawning.answer: Find trader llamas with wandering traders.

storage.answer: A llama’s strength controls its chest storage capacity; its coat color does not determine that strength.

identity.answer: This is a brown trader llama coat.

spawning.answer: Find trader llamas with wandering traders.

storage.answer: A llama’s strength controls its chest storage capacity; its coat color does not determine that strength.

spawning.answer: The tripod camera is an Education feature, not a naturally spawning Survival creature. It is not normally obtainable in standard Bedrock Survival.

interactions.answer: Its availability depends on the world and supported creator features. It is not a combat pet or a normal breeding animal.

availability.answer: The camera is associated with Education and special creator content. Do not expect an ordinary Survival crafting recipe or natural spawning biome.

identity.answer: A tripod camera is a special camera entity used in compatible Education features. It is not a normal Survival mob or a general-purpose companion.

behavior.answer: A tripod camera is a special camera entity used in compatible Education features. It is not a normal Survival mob or a general-purpose companion.

spawning.answer: Look in warm, lukewarm and deep lukewarm oceans, mangrove swamps and lush-cave water.

drops.answer: Tropical fish drop the tropical-fish item and can also drop bones in Bedrock. A living bucket of tropical fish is obtained by capturing one, not by killing it.

breeding.answer: Tropical fish cannot be bred.

taming.answer: Tropical fish cannot be tamed. Capture one with a water bucket to preserve a living fish and its appearance.

variants.answer: Bedrock has 2,700 naturally occurring tropical-fish color/pattern combinations. Bucketed fish retain their appearance, while the ordinary dropped tropical-fish item does not encode every visual combination.

sunlight.answer: Sunlight alone does not make it burn like an exposed zombie or skeleton. Other hazards, such as being out of water or changing dimensions, can still matter for the species.

fire.answer: Without protection, ordinary fire and lava can damage it. Being undead, large, or adapted to a particular biome does not by itself grant fire immunity.

spawn_conditions.answer: In Bedrock ocean spawning, check Y=50–64 and the surface-water conditions. Lush-cave aquifers can work at other heights but must count as underground. Tropical fish do not naturally spawn in every pond merely because it contains water.

leashing.answer: No, you cannot attach an ordinary lead to it through normal player interaction.

bucketing.answer: Use a water bucket directly on the creature to capture it, then use the filled bucket to release it into suitable water. Capturing and releasing it prevents ordinary natural despawning. A dispenser can release a bucketed creature but does not capture one with a water bucket.

experience.answer: It drops 1–3 experience points after a player or tamed-wolf kill. These are experience points, not player levels.

lifetime.answer: Catching it in a water bucket and releasing it prevents ordinary natural despawning. That does not prevent damage or death. A tadpole can still grow into a frog; capture is not a command to stop aging.

relocation.answer: Capture it with a water bucket, carry the filled bucket, and release it into safe water at the destination. Protect aquatic creatures from dry land. A dispenser can release a filled bucket but cannot catch a creature with a water bucket.

growth.answer: A tropicalfish has no normal baby form that grows into an adult. There is no ordinary baby-growth timer or growth food to use for this mob.

attack_style.answer: Tropical fish do not attack players. Their many colors and patterns do not create different hostile forms.

provocation.answer: A tropical fish stays passive when approached or hit. Do not confuse it with an inflating pufferfish.

counterplay.answer: Use a water bucket to collect it alive and keep it in water. Separate aquarium fish from hunters such as axolotls.

identity.answer: A tropical fish is a colorful aquatic fish with many appearance variants. Collect it alive in a water bucket for aquariums or use a bucket of tropical fish for compatible axolotl interactions.

behavior.answer: A tropical fish is a colorful aquatic fish with many appearance variants. Collect it alive in a water bucket for aquariums or use a bucket of tropical fish for compatible axolotl interactions.

combat.answer: It does not normally attack players. Collect it alive in a water bucket for aquariums or use a bucket of tropical fish for compatible axolotl interactions.

health.answer: Its normal maximum health is 3 health points (1.5 hearts). Effects can change its health during play.

water.answer: It can breathe underwater. It cannot breathe air normally, so keep it in water.

land.answer: It needs water to breathe normally. Keeping it out of water can cause suffocation damage.

identity.answer: This is the kob tropical-fish pattern, which can combine with different colors.

spawning.answer: Look for tropical fish in applicable warm/lukewarm ocean biomes, lush caves and mangrove swamps. Pattern names do not each have a separate exclusive biome.

interactions.answer: Capture a living tropical fish with a water bucket to preserve its appearance. The loose fish item is different from a bucket of living fish.
